title: Sita's swayamvara

cards: Years ago, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual, and his plow turned up something in the furrow: a baby girl, lying in the earth.

He took her home, raised her as his daughter, and named her Sita, which means furrow. A daughter of the earth itself. Now she's grown, and her father has set the test: the man who strings Shiva's bow may marry her.
Rama holds the great bow. He bends it and pulls the string toward its notch. And the bow, which no one else could even move, snaps in half with a crack like thunder.
The text says people in the hall fell to the ground from the sound.

teach.b: Today's title uses the word swayamvara. Swayam means self; vara means choice, or the chosen groom. Swayamvara: choosing for yourself, an old custom in the epics where a princess chooses her husband, often with a garland.
Here the versions part. In Valmiki's Ramayana, strictly speaking, this isn't a choosing.

teach.h: IN VALMIKI: THE PRIZE OF STRENGTH.
teach.b: Janaka had promised Sita as the prize of strength: whoever strings the bow wins her.

teach.h: IN TULSIDAS: THE GARDEN, THE GARLAND.
teach.b: But in the Ramcharitmanas, the Hindi retelling by the poet Tulsidas, there's a scene before the contest. Sita walks into a flower garden to pray and sees Rama there, picking flowers for his teacher.
She falls in love on the spot and prays to the goddess Parvati that he'll be the one. When the bow breaks, she walks forward and puts the victory garland around his neck. She chooses.
Both tellings are held dear. And in devotion, Sita is no prize at all: tradition says she is the goddess Lakshmi herself. Here's where it shows up in a Hindu home.
Devotees rarely say Rama alone. They say Sita-Ram, or Siya-Ram, with her name first.
At Ramlila and in temples the crowd shouts Siyavar Ramachandra ki jai: victory to Ramachandra, Sita's groom. Vara again, the same word as in swayamvara.
Hindus often worship God as a couple, Sita-Ram, Radha-Krishna, Lakshmi-Narayan, and the goddess's name usually comes first.
And when a Hindu bride and groom exchange garlands at a wedding today, the jaimala, many families think of this scene.

how: The wedding of Rama and Sita is celebrated as Vivah Panchami in parts of India and Nepal, especially around Janakpur; the breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila, and Hindu weddings keep a garland exchange, the jaimala.

games.q: you're Sita, in Tulsidas's telling. the day before the contest, you see a young stranger picking flowers in the garden. what do you do?
o: forget him; the bow will decide.
pray to Parvati that he'll be the one.
tell your father to cancel the contest.
games.why: she prays to Parvati. when the bow breaks, she garlands Rama: the choice she'd already made in the garden.

practice: Many Hindus chant the two names together: Sita Ram, Sita Ram. Try it softly with your breath for a minute or two, her name, then his.
If you don't pray, think of two people you can't picture apart, two grandparents, two friends, and notice whose name you say first, and why.

wordCard.voice: Sita's swayamvara. Rama breaks Shiva's bow, and in Tulsidas's telling Sita garlands him: her choice, made first in a garden.

orig.note: Sanskrit: self (svayam) choice (vara), a bride choosing her groom.

carryVoice: Your line: Sita-Ram, her name comes first. In one telling the garland was hers to give, and devotees still say her name before his. Until tomorrow.
